title: Etiquette & language
body:
Izumo Taisha breaks the standard shrine ritual: everywhere else in Japan it's two bows, two claps, one bow — here it's two bows, four claps, one bow. The shrine's own explanation ties it to the annual grand festival's eight claps (an old symbol of the infinite), halved for everyday worship. Don't default to the two-clap pattern out of habit; it's the one shrine on this trip where that reads as the wrong move, not a shortcut.

Shimane's regional dialect (Izumo-ben in the east, Iwami-ben around Oda/Omori) is distinct enough that standard-Japanese phrasebooks sound a little formal to locals — nobody will mind, but don't expect textbook responses back.

Basic courtesy carries the rest: remove shoes wherever there's a raised floor or tatami (soba houses, ryokan, machiya inns), don't eat while walking through the Omori townscape, and keep voices down in residential lanes — people still live in those Edo-period houses.
